text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The Centre Party re-elected its controversial leader Olof Johansson but several members did not join the applause following the election.

- Most government employee unions in Europe support the economic and monetary union (EMU) but to get public support the project cannot increase unemployment, says Inger Efraimsson, chairwoman of Swedish white collar municipality union SKTF, and Rodney Bickerstaffe, secretary-general of the British union Unison, in a column.

- High Swedish wage increases worry Svante Oberg, who has been appointed by the government to look into how to improve the system. Oberg said the system has structural problems which pushes wage increases higher than in other countries despite the country's high unemployment.
- The attempt to raise pulp prices to $630 per tonne seems unrealistic as North American and Scandinavian pulp stocks (NorScan) have not fallen as much as expected, a newspaper analysis shows.

- Peder Sager Wallenberg, member of the powerful Swedish Wallenberg family, has built up a group of Information Technology (IT) companies in Sweden and the U.S. that has an annual turnover of more than one billion crowns. He has recently moved back to Sweden from Britain.
- Domestic Swedish airline Transwede expects to reach break even for the first six months of the year and for the full-year its chief executive Per Odegaard hopes for a profit.

- Foreign investors do not care which bourse list shares are traded on but focus on a share's liquidity. Several Swedish companies have recently moved from the Stockholm Stock Exchange's main A list to the smaller O list for tax reasons.
